parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by the centre of gravity of an object.

markscheme_points.text: point where (all) the weight (of the object) is taken to act

hints: Hint 1: Think of the weight of an object as made up of lots of tiny weights on every particle - where could you imagine all of that combined weight pulling down from?
parts.proper_answer: The point where all the weight of the object is taken to act.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Centre of Gravity Really Means**
Imagine breaking the rod or any object into thousands of tiny pieces. Each tiny piece has its own tiny weight pulling down. It would be very messy to deal with them all separately, so we replace them with one single weight acting at one special point. That point is the centre of gravity.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A non-uniform rod $XY$ is pivoted at point $P$, as shown in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

The rod has length $4.00\text{ m}$ and weight $44.0\text{ N}$. The centre of gravity of the rod is $1.70\text{ m}$ from end $X$ of the rod. Point $P$ is $1.10\text{ m}$ from end $X$.

A sphere hangs by a wire from end $Y$ of the rod. The weight of the sphere is $3.0\text{ N}$. The weight of the wire is negligible.

A force $F$ is applied vertically downwards at end $X$ so that the horizontal rod is in equilibrium.

parts.label: (b)(i)

markscheme_points.guidance: 1 mark for any one correct moment and 2 marks for two correct moments

hints: Hint 1: Focus on point P as the pivot. Work out how far each of the three downward forces is from P, and decide whether each one on its own would turn the rod clockwise or anticlockwise about P.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Each Distance From P**
You are sitting with the diagram. P is 1.10 m from X. The rod weight 44.0 N acts at its centre of gravity 1.70 m from X, so its distance from P is $1.70 - 1.10 = 0.60\text{ m}$ to the right of P. The sphere weight 3.0 N acts at Y, 4.00 m from X, so its distance from P is $4.00 - 1.10 = 2.90\text{ m}$ to the right of P. $F$ is $1.10\text{ m}$ to the left of P.

Step 2: **Balance Clockwise Against Anticlockwise**
For equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments about P equals the sum of anticlockwise moments. $F$ pulling down on the left tries to turn the rod anticlockwise about P, while the 44.0 N and 3.0 N weights on the right try to turn it clockwise. So: $$F \times 1.10 = (44.0 \times 0.60) + (3.0 \times 2.90)$$ $$F \times 1.10 = 26.4 + 8.7 = 35.1$$ $$F = \frac{35.1}{1.10} = 32\text{ N (to 2 s.f.)}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the force exerted on the rod by the pivot.
hints: Hint 1: The rod is not moving up or down, so the total upward force must balance the total downward force - think about which forces push down and which one must push up.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Balance Forces Vertically**
In equilibrium the resultant force is zero. All three weights $F$, 44.0 N and 3.0 N act downwards on the rod, so the pivot must push upwards to balance them. Let the pivot force be $R$ upwards: $$R = F + 44.0 + 3.0$$ $$R = 32 + 44.0 + 3.0 = 79\text{ N}$$ So the pivot exerts about $79\text{ N}$ upwards on the rod.

parts.label: (c)
(c)(i)
parts.text: Use Archimedes' principle to determine the radius $r$ of the sphere.
hints: Hint 1: Recall what Archimedes tells you about upthrust - it equals the weight of the fluid pushed aside by the sphere, which links upthrust to fluid density and displaced volume.
Hint 2: You know upthrust, liquid density and $g$, so think how you can rearrange that link to first find the volume of the sphere.
Hint 3: Once you have the volume, remember the geometry of a sphere connects $V$ to radius $r$ - check how to isolate $r$ from that relation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Upthrust to Find Volume**
Archimedes principle says upthrust equals weight of displaced liquid. For a fully immersed sphere, displaced volume equals sphere volume $V$: $$\text{upthrust} = \rho g V$$ Rearrange for $V$: $$V = \frac{\text{upthrust}}{\rho g} = \frac{2.5}{1100 \times 9.81}$$ $$V = 2.32 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3$$

Step 2: **Use Sphere Volume to Find Radius**
Volume of a sphere is: $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$ Rearrange for $r$: $$r^3 = \frac{3V}{4\pi}$$ $$r = \left[\frac{3 \times 2.32 \times 10^{-4}}{4\pi}\right]^{1/3}$$ $$r = 0.038\text{ m (to 2 s.f.)}$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant moment of the forces on the rod about $P$.

markscheme_points.text: resultant moment = 2.5 × 2.9 or resultant moment = F × 1.1 − (44 × 0.6 + 0.5 × 2.9)
= 7.3 N m (allow 7.2 N m or 7.4 N m from rounded values of F); direction: anticlockwise

hints: Hint 1: The upthrust lifts the sphere, so the downward pull at end Y is no longer 3.0 N - think about what the new effective downward force at Y becomes.
Hint 2: Now compare the anticlockwise moment from $F$ about P with the new smaller clockwise moments - which side wins and by how much?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the New Force at Y**
Upthrust of 2.5 N acts upwards on the sphere, while its weight 3.0 N acts downwards. The net downward pull on the rod at Y is: $$3.0 - 2.5 = 0.50\text{ N}$$ $F$ is unchanged at about 32 N.

Step 2: **Calculate Resultant Moment About P**
Take anticlockwise as positive. Anticlockwise moment from $F$: $$F \times 1.10 = 32 \times 1.10$$ Clockwise moments from rod and sphere: $$(44.0 \times 0.60) + (0.50 \times 2.90)$$ Resultant: $$\text{resultant} = (32 \times 1.10) - [(44.0 \times 0.60) + (0.50 \times 2.90)]$$ $$\text{resultant} = 35.2 - 27.85 = 7.3\text{ N m}$$ Since the $F$ side is larger, the resultant is anticlockwise. The rod is no longer in equilibrium.
